analysis.one_liner: Gives state and local public employees a federal right to form unions and bargain collectively.
analysis.headline: With 181 cosponsors, including 8 Republicans, the bill never received a hearing or a vote and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set a federal minimum standard of collective bargaining rights for state and local government workers — the right to form a union, bargain over wages and working conditions, have union dues deducted from paychecks, and settle contract disputes through binding arbitration. The Federal Labor Relations Authority would judge whether each state's laws meet that standard; states that fall short would have their public-sector bargaining run by the federal authority after a transition period. States with adequate laws would keep their own systems untouched.
analysis.who_benefits: Public employees — teachers, nurses, EMTs, firefighters, transit and municipal workers — in the many states that today give them little or no legal right to bargain, who would gain a federally enforced right to organize and negotiate. Labor unions would gain members and dues as new workplaces became organized. Public employers and unions that already bargain under strong state laws would keep their existing arrangements, since the bill leaves compliant states alone [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Public workers in states without bargaining rights

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federal floor of bargaining rights for state and local government employees: the right to organize, join or assist a union, bargain collectively through representatives of their own choosing, and engage in concerted activity, with unions recognized by majority vote and contracts put in writing.
Requires payroll deduction of union dues once an employee agrees to it, and bars employers from interfering with or coercing workers exercising these rights.
Gives negotiations a way to end: an impasse mechanism such as mediation, fact-finding, or arbitration that culminates in a binding resolution, so a stubborn employer cannot simply stall forever.

Enforces the rights in the real world: the Federal Labor Relations Authority could hold hearings, issue subpoenas, and order compliance, and workers could go to federal court after 180 days if the Authority does not act, with attorneys' fees available.

States that already substantially provide these rights keep their own systems — the bill does not preempt them — and states get a transition period of at least two years, or until the end of their next legislative session, before federal rules take over.

analysis.who_pays: State and local governments, and ultimately their taxpayers, who as employers would face binding arbitration of contract disputes, federal administration of elections and complaints in states with weak labor laws, and the fiscal cost of whatever wages and benefits arbitrators award. States would also cede part of their control over public-workforce policy to a federal agency [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: State and local governments and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: It overrides state labor policy: a federal agency would judge each state's laws and, where they fall short, take over public-sector bargaining, which is a significant shift of power away from states and their voters.

Binding arbitration of contract disputes means unelected arbitrators could set wages and benefits, shifting costs onto state and local budgets and taxpayers rather than leaving those decisions to elected officials.

The same bill that grants bargaining rights bans emergency services employees and law enforcement officers from striking, lockouts, or job actions that would disrupt emergency or public safety services, removing those workers' strongest form of leverage.
Small towns are carved out: a state may exempt political subdivisions with fewer than 5,000 people or fewer than 25 employees, so some public workers would remain uncovered.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the millions of public workers in states without bargaining rights, the gains are large: enforceable union rights, dues deduction, and a dispute process that ends in a binding decision. The costs are real but narrower — states lose some control over workforce policy, taxpayers could bear arbitrator-ordered pay and benefit increases, and emergency and law enforcement personnel would trade away the right to strike. A fair accounting favors the workers, though the federal preemption of state labor law is the strongest good-faith objection.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never scheduled a hearing or vote, and it expired when the congressional session ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Matt Cartwright introduced the bill on May 16, 2024, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day.
It attracted 181 cosponsors — 173 of the House's 216 Democrats and 8 of the 224 Republicans — including Representatives Fitzpatrick, Pocan, Norcross, and Dingell among the original backers.
The committee took no further action: no hearing, no markup, no vote was ever scheduled, and the bill died there when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State and local governments in states without public-sector bargaining laws keep their current rules, and no public employer will face federal arbitration or administration. Public workers in those states gained nothing.

for.name: Matt Cartwright
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 87 original cosponsors, including Republicans Fitzpatrick, Bacon, Chavez-DeRemer, Lawler, Molinaro, and Mullin.

for.name: 173 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, roughly four-fifths of the House Democratic caucus.

for.name: 8 of 224 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, a small bipartisan contingent led by Rep. Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania.

against.name: Virginia Foxx
against.role: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after it was referred to her committee.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Democratic — 173 of 216 House Democrats signed on versus only 8 of 224 Republicans — and the Republican-run committee where it sat took no action.

industries.note: The bill would make labor organizations the permanent, federally protected channel for public employees to bargain: recognition is hard to undo without a 30% employee petition, and dues deduction is guaranteed once an employee agrees. It also expands their reach into states where public-sector bargaining barely exists today, while restricting strikes by emergency and law enforcement members.

As employers, state and local governments would lose the discretion to refuse bargaining, could not stall negotiations past binding arbitration, and in states with weak labor laws would have their labor relations run by a federal agency. Their interest in resisting these rules ran directly against workers' interest in gaining them.

The small federal agency that currently handles labor relations only for federal employees would take on a sweeping new docket: judging every state's laws, supervising elections, and enforcing bargaining rights for state and local workers nationwide.
